title: Address Binding & Address Spaces
summary: Why every process thinks it owns memory starting at address 0, and the three points in a program's life where a logical address gets tied to a physical one.

slides.markdown:
Run two copies of the same program and both will report their code starts at the same address — say `0x400000`. That isn't a coincidence or a bug: each process lives in its own **logical address space**, and something translates those addresses to real, non-overlapping physical memory behind the scenes.

That something is **address binding**, and it can happen at three different times: compile time, load time, or run time. Which one a system picks determines whether a program can be relocated after it starts running — the foundation everything else in memory management builds on.

A **logical address** (also called a virtual address) is what a running program uses — the value in its instruction pointer, the pointer it dereferences. A **physical address** is the actual row-and-column location in RAM that the memory controller reads or writes.

These are almost never the same number. Your program's pointer might read `0x400000`, but the byte it refers to could physically sit at `0x7f3a12000000` in RAM, depending on where the OS decided to load that process this time.

The CPU never lets a user process touch a physical address directly — every memory access a program makes is a logical address that gets translated before it reaches the memory bus.

slides.sectionTitle: Why programs don't use physical addresses directly
slides.markdown:
If a compiler baked real physical addresses into a program, that program could only ever run when those exact physical bytes were free — impossible to guarantee once multiple programs share one machine.

Logical addresses solve three problems at once: **relocation** (the OS can load a process anywhere in RAM, or move it later), **protection** (a process literally cannot form a pointer to another process's physical memory, because it never sees physical addresses at all), and **multiprogramming** (many processes can each believe they own address `0` without colliding).

This indirection is the single idea underneath paging, segmentation, and virtual memory — they're all just different ways of doing logical-to-physical translation.

slides.sectionTitle: Address binding: compile time, load time, execution time
slides.markdown:
**Address binding** is the act of committing a logical address to an actual location. It can happen at three points:

- **Compile time** — the compiler emits absolute addresses directly, assuming the program will always load at one fixed spot. Rare today (some tiny embedded/bootloader code still does this); if the load address ever changes, the binary must be recompiled.
- **Load time** — the compiler emits *relocatable* addresses (offsets from an unknown base); the loader picks a base address when the program starts and patches the offsets in. The load address is fixed once running, but can differ between runs.
- **Execution (run) time** — binding is deferred until the instruction actually executes, via hardware. The program can be **moved during execution** — from one region of memory to another, or partially to disk and back — because every access is translated fresh, every time.

Modern general-purpose OSes use execution-time binding almost exclusively, because it's the only option compatible with paging and swapping.

slides.sectionTitle: The MMU: translating logical to physical at runtime
slides.markdown:
Execution-time binding needs hardware fast enough to translate on every single memory access without crushing performance. That hardware is the **Memory Management Unit (MMU)** — a component built into the CPU core.

Every load, store, and instruction fetch a user process issues goes through the MMU first: the CPU emits a logical address, the MMU consults its translation state (a base/limit pair in the simplest case, a page table in the general case) and produces a physical address, and only *that* address reaches the memory bus.

Because this happens on every access, the MMU has to be fast — nanoseconds, not microseconds — which is why translation state is cached in hardware (the TLB, covered later) rather than looked up from scratch each time.

slides.sectionTitle: Base and limit registers — the simplest relocation and protection scheme
slides.markdown:
The simplest possible MMU uses two registers per running process: a **base register** (where this process's memory starts physically) and a **limit register** (how big its region is).

Translation is one addition: `physical = base + logical`. Protection is one comparison: if `logical >= limit`, the hardware traps instead of completing the access — a process literally cannot construct an address that reaches outside its own region.

On a context switch, the OS just reloads base and limit for the next process — cheap, but it only supports one contiguous region per process, which is exactly the limitation contiguous allocation and, later, paging exist to remove.

slides.sectionTitle: Worked example: translating with base and limit
slides.markdown:
A process has `base = 0x14000` and `limit = 0x3000` (12 KB). It issues logical address `0x1500`.

```text
Step 1: bounds check
  0x1500 < limit (0x3000)?  yes -> allowed

Step 2: translate
  physical = base + logical
           = 0x14000 + 0x1500
           = 0x15500
```

Now the same process issues `0x3500` (past its limit):

```text
Step 1: bounds check
  0x3500 < limit (0x3000)?  no -> trap
  Result: hardware fault, OS delivers SIGSEGV
```

Every real MMU — paged or segmented — is doing a more elaborate version of exactly these two steps: check the access is allowed, then compute the physical address.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: confusing address binding with paging
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Address binding is basically another name for paging."

**Why it's wrong:** paging is one specific *mechanism* for doing execution-time binding — splitting memory into fixed-size pages and frames, with a page table doing the translation. But execution-time binding existed before paging (base/limit registers are execution-time binding too) and doesn't require pages at all.

**Correct model:** address binding is the general question of *when* a logical address gets tied to a physical one. Paging, segmentation, and base/limit registers are three different *how*s for execution-time binding specifically. Keep the "when" (binding time) and the "how" (translation mechanism) as separate axes.

slides.sectionTitle: The senior nuance: why binding time matters for security, not just relocation
slides.markdown:
A junior answer stops at "execution-time binding allows relocation." A staff-level answer connects it to security: **Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR)** relies entirely on execution-time binding. Because the OS can place a process's stack, heap, and shared libraries at a fresh, randomized base on every launch, an attacker who finds a buffer-overflow bug can't hardcode the address of a useful gadget — they don't know where anything landed this run.

This is also why statically-bound, fixed-address code (old-style non-PIE binaries, some embedded firmware) is considered a security liability today: predictable addresses make exploit development dramatically easier. Position-Independent Executables (PIE) exist specifically so user-space code can be relocated at load time and randomized, the same execution-time-binding idea applied to defense.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: the three binding times at a glance
slides.markdown:
| | Compile time | Load time | Execution time |
|---|---|---|---|
| Who binds | Compiler | Loader | MMU hardware, continuously |
| Load address | Fixed forever | Fixed per run, chosen at load | Never fixed — can change mid-run |
| Needs hardware support | No | No | Yes (MMU) |
| Supports moving a running process | No | No | Yes (basis for swapping, paging) |
| Real-world use today | Rare (some bootloaders/firmware) | Static-linked simple binaries | Virtually all general-purpose OSes |

The trend across the table is one direction: pushing the binding decision later buys flexibility (relocation, protection, randomization) at the cost of needing dedicated hardware to pay for it on every access.
